title: Sampling, Probability, and Inference
summary: Set the sample size, yes count, and school size, and watch one fraction act as an estimate, a probability, and a tree of two picks.
narration: Your school wants to know if anyone would use the library on a Saturday, and there is no time to ask everyone. So you ask a small group picked at random, and one fraction does three jobs at once. It estimates the whole school, it marks a spot on the 0-to-1 probability scale, and multiplied by itself it gives the chance that two picks both say yes. Slide the controls and watch all three readings move together.

practice.prompt: A random sample of 40 students at a school of 720 finds that 18 of them walk to school. Based on this sample, about how many of the 720 students walk to school?
practice.explanation: The sample proportion is 18/40 = 9/20 = 0.45. Treat that as the school-wide fraction: 0.45 x 720 = 324. (Check by scaling: 720 / 40 = 18 groups of 40, and 18 x 18 = 324.)

practice.prompt: In a random sample, 3 out of every 5 students said yes. Using that sample as your probability model, you pick a student at random, put the name back, and pick again. What is the probability that both picks say yes? Give a decimal.
practice.explanation: P(yes) = 3/5 = 0.6 for each pick, and the two picks are independent, so P(both yes) = 3/5 x 3/5 = 9/25 = 0.36.

practice.prompt: Two random samples of 10 students each record their daily reading minutes. Sample A has a mean of 25 minutes and a mean absolute deviation of 5 minutes; sample B has a mean of 40 minutes and the same MAD of 5 minutes. How many MADs apart are the two centers?
practice.explanation: The gap between the centers is 40 - 25 = 15 minutes. Express it in units of the typical spread: 15 / 5 = 3, so the centers are 3 MADs apart. (15 is the raw gap in minutes, 5 is the MAD itself, and 1.5 divides the gap by the sample size instead of by the MAD.)
